blocks.text: We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.

blocks.text: Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.

blocks.text: So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. CLAUDE.md

tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.
REVIEW.md

, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.

blocks.text: Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. blocks.text: We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. blocks.text: Code review's second job has always been to spread codebase understanding. Reading a teammate's diff is how you learn what changed and how the pieces fit. If machines do most of the reading, how does anyone learn the code?

blocks.text: "YOU LAND IT, YOU OWN IT"

inlines.text: "YOU LAND IT, YOU OWN IT"

blocks.text: If you land a small or medium change and something still goes wrong, it's a team norm that you usually fix it. A few things keep this from going badly:

inlines.text: If you land a small or medium change and something still goes wrong, it's a team norm that you usually fix it. A few things keep this from going badly:
Changes are small,
so they're easy to review, debug and revert.
Everything is reversible.
Flags, reverts and staged releases undo most mistakes in minutes.
Blast radius sets the bar.
Expensive code gets more people and more checks.
Regressions surface fast
through telemetry and internal use.
It isn't blame.
Owning a fix means you have the most context; incident reviews look at the system.

blocks.text: Ownership is also shared. Much of the team works in open channels where anyone can see what others are building, pick up a thread, or point a Claude at a gap, and feedback comes from people who don't own the code too. That openness is a big part of how quality stays high without a gate on every line.

Add a

blocks.text: On every pull request

inlines.text: On every pull request
Require CI, and add "Testing", "Risk" and "How to revert" to your PR template.
Add an AI reviewer (Code Review for Claude Code, or the Claude Code GitHub Action) on one repo, tune
REVIEW.md
for a few weeks, then widen.
Add automated security review, and require every review thread resolved before merge.
Match review effort to risk: a quick pass on routine changes, a deep one where a missed bug is expensive (Quick, Standard or Deep in Code Review).
Cap review rounds; after the first few, re-review only the new diff.

blocks.text: Approval

inlines.text: Approval
Write down risk tiers, set from the change rather than the author; start strict and loosen with evidence.
Keep the lighter approval paths for authors you trust.
Use CODEOWNERS and branch protection so auth, billing, CI and release workflows, and installers always need a person.
Never let a bot's approval replace a required human's; dismiss approvals on new commits.

blocks.text: Merge and after

inlines.text: Merge and after
Use a merge queue, feature flags, internal use first, staged releases and one-step rollback.
Turn incidents and reverts into an eval set, and rescore the reviewer whenever its prompts, tools or model change.
Measure human time, with revert and incident rates as the guardrail.
